prompt: Read the image file {path}. It is a crop of one column of a printed 1854 Hebrew-English lexicon (Gesenius, Robinson translation). Transcribe every complete printed text line exactly, one array element per printed line, top to bottom. Preserve spelling, capitalisation, punctuation, printed abbreviations, section marks and end-of-line hyphenation. Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Syriac, Greek and Ethiopic must be Unicode text with every visible vowel point, dagesh, accent and diacritic, written in logical order with no bidi control characters; keep the words of a right-to-left phrase in the order they are read, and keep the printed left-to-right order of separate items in a list. Where a page or column header, page number or catchword is present, include it as its own line. If a line is only partially visible at the top or bottom edge, omit it entirely rather than guessing. Never add, reorder, translate, normalise or omit anything that is fully visible. If the crop contains no text, return an empty array.

lines: קיט
קיק
קַיִט Chald. m. i. q. Heb. קַיִץ, sum-
mer, Dan. 2, 35.
קִיטוֹר m. (r. קָטַר I ) 1. smoke, Gen.
2. vapour, a cloud, Ps. 148, 8.
קִים m. (r. קוּם) a rising up against
any one, see the root no. 1. c ; hence
concr. Job 22, 20 קִימָנוּ our adversaries,
enemies, i. q. קָמֵינוּ.
קְיָם Chald. m. a statute, edict, Dan. 6,
8. In Targ. often for Heb. חֹק, בְּרִית.
Syr. ܩܝܳܡܳܐ. R. קוּם.
קַיָּם Chald. adj. enduring, sure, Dan.
4, 23. Syr. ܩܰܝܳܡܳܐ id. R. קוּם.
קִימָה f. (r. קוּם) a rising up, Lam.
קִימוֹשׂ, see קִמּוֹשׂ.
קִין see in r. קוּן.
קַיִן m. (r. קוּן) 1. a lance, spear, c.
suff. קֵינוֹ 2 Sam. 21, 16.
2. Cain, pr. n. a) The eldest son of
Adam, the murderer of his brother Abel,
Gen. 4, 1 sq. Among his posterity were
the inventors of arts and arms. The
name comes from r. קוּן, perh. lance, as
a murderous weapon; though in Gen.
4, 1 the etymology is explained as if r.
קוּן were i. q. קָנָה no. 1, viz. she bore
Cain and said: I have gotten (borne) a
man with the help of the Lord. b)
The tribe of the Kenites, Num. 24, 22.
Judg. 4, 11; see קֵינִי. c) A town in
the tribe of Judah, c. art. Josh. 15, 57.
קִינָה f. (r. קוּן) plur. קִינוֹת, once קִינִים
1. song, Syr. ܩܺܝܢܬܳܐ musical sound,
song. Spec. a song of mourning, lamen-
tation, Jer. 9, 9. Am. 5, 1. 8, 10. Ez. 2,
2. Kinah, pr. n. of a town in Judah
Sam. 30, 29, also קִנִי 2 Sam. 27, 10 קֵינִי
1 Chr. 2, 55, gentile n. Kenite, collect.
the Kenites, a Canaanitish tribe dwell-
ing among the Amalekites, 1 Sam. 15,
6, comp. Num. 24, 20. 21. Hobab. the
father-in-law of Moses, was phylarch of
one of their tribes, Judg. 1, 16. 4, 11.
The family of Heber the Kenite dwelt
in Naphtali, Judg. 4, 11. See too קַיִן
no. 2. b.—Syr. ܩܰܝܢܳܝܳܐ id. pr. ‘a smith,’
and this is prob. the signif. of Heb. קֵינִי,
from r. קוּן.
קֵינָן (smith, perh. lancer, r. קוּן) Ke-
nan or Cainan, pr. n. of an antediluvian
patriarch descended from Seth, Gen. 5,
קַיִץ m. (r. קוּץ III ) c. suff. קֵיצְךָ, har-
vest of fruits, fruit-harvest, not of grain
which is קָצִיר; pr. the cutting off of
fruit. Is. 16, 9. Jer. 8, 20. 48, 32. Spec.
fig-harvest, which in Palestine takes
place in August; although early figs
(בִּכּוּרִים) ripen at the summer solstice ;
Is. 28, 4 as the early fig before the har-
vest. Mic. 7, 1.—Hence
a) the harvest-time of figs, i. e. sum-
mer, espec. midsummer, the hottest sea-
son ; Arab. قَيْظ or قَوْظ mid-summer.
Chald. קַיִט, Syr. ܩܰܝܛܳܐ, id.—Ps. 32, 4
בְּחַרְבוֹנֵי קַיִץ into the droughts of sum-
בֵּית הַקַּיִץ the summer-house Am. 3, 15.
Sometimes it seems to include the spring,
as חֹרֶף also includes autumn and win-
ter; see in חֹרֶף.
b) fruit, spec. figs, as harvested, Am.
8, 1. 2; comp. Jer. 24, 1 sq. Jerome po-
ma, which is a general word including
figs; see the lexicons. 2 Sam. 16, 1 מֵאָה
קַיִץ, ellipt. for מֵאָה דְּבֵלוֹת קַיִץ, a hun-
dred cakes of figs. Comp. in Engl. the
harvest for the grain harvested.
קִיצוֹן m. adj. (r. קָצַץ; for קִצּוֹן, after
the analogy of חִיצוֹן from חוּץ, Dag.
om. after ־ִי) the last, the extreme, only
קִיקָיוֹן m. Jon. 4, 6–10, according to
Jerome, the Talmud, and Heb. intpp.
the ricinus, palma Christi, Arab. الخروع
el-kherû'a, Egyptian κίκι, κούκι, Diod.
Sic. 1. 34, a tall biennial plant still culti-
vated in gardens, of an elegant appear-
ance and rapid growth, with a stalk or
trunk full of sap. At Jericho it becomes
a considerable tree; see Bibl. Res. in
Palest. II. p. 281. Bochart. Hieroz. II.
p. 293. 623. Celsii Hierobot. II. p. 273
sq. Thesaur. p. 1214.—According to
Sept. and Peshito, a gourd.
